questions.q: What is the key difference between bitsandbytes and GPTQ/AWQ?
options: bitsandbytes only supports INT8, while GPTQ and AWQ only support INT4
bitsandbytes quantizes with no calibration dataset; GPTQ and AWQ both run a calibration pass first
GPTQ and AWQ require retraining the entire model from scratch
bitsandbytes is slower to load than GPTQ or AWQ
questions.explain: bitsandbytes quantizes at load time with no calibration data. GPTQ and AWQ both calibrate on sample data first, which is what lets them compress further with less accuracy loss.

questions.q: How does GPTQ limit the accuracy loss from rounding weights to a lower bit-width?
options: It skips quantizing any weight it judges important
It quantizes one layer at a time and uses remaining weights to compensate for rounding error, guided by Hessian information
It retrains the full model after quantizing
It only ever quantizes to 8-bit, never lower
questions.explain: GPTQ quantizes layer by layer and, after rounding each weight, adjusts the not-yet-quantized weights to compensate for the introduced error based on second-order sensitivity information.

questions.q: What does 'activation-aware' mean in AWQ's approach?
options: AWQ only quantizes activations, never weights
AWQ identifies weight channels tied to unusually large activation values and protects them during quantization
AWQ requires the model to be retrained with new activation functions
AWQ ignores activations entirely and only looks at weight magnitude
questions.explain: AWQ looks at activation magnitudes during calibration to find the small set of 'salient' weight channels, then scales them to minimize their precision loss when quantized.

questions.q: What is the main practical trade-off between INT8 and INT4 quantization?
options: INT8 and INT4 always produce identical accuracy and memory savings
INT4 roughly doubles memory usage compared to INT8
INT8 keeps more memory footprint but loses less accuracy; INT4 saves far more memory but is more sensitive to quantization method quality
INT4 is only usable on CPUs, never GPUs
questions.explain: INT8 is the conservative choice — modest savings, minimal accuracy loss. INT4 roughly halves memory again, which can be the difference in GPU count needed, but accuracy risk rises without good calibration.

questions.q: Why does calibration-based error correction (as in GPTQ and AWQ) matter more at 4-bit than at 8-bit?
options: It doesn't — calibration provides identical benefit at any bit-width
8-bit quantization is never used in practice, so the comparison is moot
The narrower the representable range, the more naive rounding error accumulates, so careful calibration has more accuracy to recover
Calibration only works at 4-bit due to a hardware limitation
questions.explain: At lower bit-widths the available range to represent values shrinks, so rounding error from naive quantization grows — which is exactly where GPTQ's and AWQ's calibration-based corrections pay off most.
